rationale:
Evidence: iteration 5 (score 137.76) is the best measured design. It is iteration 2's geometry and controller with base_speed raised from 1.6 to 1.8. That speed step added about 5.8 points, and the single oval finish (1.88 s at base 1.6) shows time margin on that track. Every trial still ends off track with max_error at about 0.06 m and rms_error at about 0.03 m. Line loss remains 0.65 to 0.8 per run on the s-bend and slalom.

What I accepted from the round-1 critique: (1) The critique is right that my draft changed several things at once. A wheel_track change is mainly a gain change (about 20% more yaw per unit of command), and the draft's four-field geometry change could not be attributed. I reject the draft as written. (2) The critique is right that ki 1.0 is outside the tested range and that ki 0.6 already scored lower than ki 0.3. I reject ki 1.0 and ki 0. (3) The critique is right that the body_width argument is vacuous below 0.19 m, and that the identical iteration 2 and 4 scores need checking. I keep the iteration-5 geometry because it is the best-evidenced geometry.

What I changed: base_speed from 1.8 to 2.0, the top of the useful range (above 2.0 nothing changes). Everything else is identical to iteration 5, so this is a single-variable test. The 3 s limit needs about 1.5 m/s average, and a faster base is the only lever that targets the completion and time terms (500 plus up to 60 points) without a new unverified gain.

Expected result: at least as much progress as iteration 5 (oval about 0.55), some reduction in completion_time on runs that stay on track, and possibly more off-track ends if lateral load is the limit. Decision rule for the next round: if progress rises and the run stays on track, keep 2.0 and test whether s-bend and slalom line-loss events fall. If progress falls or off-track ends rise sooner, return to 1.8 and test one sensor footprint or span change on the s-bend and slalom. If max_error still reaches 0.06 with flat rms, the next single test is ki 0.1, not ki 1.0.
